title: Seeds highest in magnesium, calcium and iron

seo.title: Seeds highest in magnesium, calcium and iron
seo.meta_description: Compare hemp, pumpkin, sesame, chia and sunflower seeds per 30 g. Hemp leads magnesium; whole sesame leads calcium and iron.
seo.search_intent: Find which common seeds provide the most magnesium, calcium and iron

excerpt: No single seed wins every mineral. Per 30 g, hulled hemp provides about 210 mg magnesium and pumpkin seeds about 150 mg. For calcium, whole sesame stands out at roughly 293 mg and chia at 189 mg. Whole sesame also leads iron at about 4.4 mg per 30 g. Hull removal and processing can dramatically change sesame calcium.
content_html:
Calling a seed ‘mineral-rich’ is incomplete unless you name the mineral. Hemp stands out for magnesium, whole sesame for calcium and iron, and chia ranks especially high for calcium.

The table uses 30 g portions and unsalted references. The forms are stated because they are not perfectly identical: hemp is hulled while the sesame reference is whole and dried.

30 gMagnesiumCalciumIron
Hulled hemp210 mg21 mg2.4 mg
Raw pumpkin seeds150 mg11 mg2.5 mg
Whole dried sesame105 mg293 mg4.4 mg
Dried chia101 mg189 mg2.3 mg
Raw sunflower kernels91 mg35 mg1.3 mg

Magnesium: hemp and pumpkin seeds

Hulled hemp provides about 700 mg magnesium/100 g and pumpkin seeds about 500 mg. Thirty grams supplies roughly 210 and 150 mg. Sesame and chia both land near 100–105 mg per 30 g.

Calcium: whole sesame needs context

At 975 mg/100 g, whole sesame clearly leads this table, followed by chia at 631 mg. But much of sesame's calcium sits in the hull. A hulled tahini can contain dramatically less, so the whole-seed number should not be transferred to every sesame product.

Iron: sesame, then pumpkin and hemp

Whole sesame provides about 14.6 mg iron/100 g; pumpkin seeds 8.36 mg; hemp 7.95 mg; chia 7.72 mg. At 30 g, pumpkin, hemp and chia cluster around 2.3–2.5 mg.

Content is not the same as absorption

These figures describe mineral present in the food, not how much the body absorbs. Phytate and other plant compounds can reduce mineral bioavailability. Pairing plant iron with vitamin C can improve non-heme iron absorption.

Phytate helps explain why mineral content and mineral absorption are not identical. Seeds naturally store phosphorus in phytate, which can bind some iron, zinc, calcium, and magnesium. This does not make seeds poor foods; it simply means the number on a composition table is not the same as the amount the body absorbs.

Processing can change availability. Soaking, sprouting, fermenting, grinding, and roasting can alter phytate levels or make minerals easier to access, although the effect varies by seed and method. Tahini, for example, behaves differently from whole sesame because the seed is ground and sometimes hulled.

Calcium in sesame deserves special context. Whole unhulled sesame can contain a large amount, but much of it sits in the hull and bioavailability is limited. Hulled sesame may show less calcium on paper. A high milligram value should therefore not automatically be treated as equivalent to dairy or a fortified drink.

Serving size keeps the numbers realistic. Two tablespoons of seeds can enrich a meal with magnesium, iron, healthy fats, and protein, but they are not normally eaten in 100-gram portions. Using several seed types across meals may be more practical than trying to obtain every mineral from the one that ranks first.

Vitamin C can improve absorption of non-heme iron from plant foods. Adding fruit, peppers, tomatoes, broccoli, or another vitamin-C-rich food to a meal with seeds is a simple way to support iron uptake. Tea and coffee taken with the meal can have the opposite effect for some non-heme iron.

Grinding seeds can make them easier to incorporate into food and may improve access to some nutrients, but ground products expose more surface to oxygen. Keeping ground flax, sesame meal, or seed mixes sealed and cool helps protect flavor and unsaturated fats.

Seeds also bring substantial unsaturated fat and energy, which is nutritionally useful but easy to overlook when focusing only on minerals. A spoonful sprinkled on vegetables, yogurt, soup, or oats can improve nutrient density without requiring a very large portion. That approach makes mineral-rich seeds an addition to a varied diet rather than a concentrated supplement-like dose.

Serving size keeps the ranking useful

Thirty grams of seeds generally provides roughly 150–200 calories. A 5 g sprinkle will not deliver the same mineral amounts as the table, and eating 100 g solely to chase one mineral is rarely necessary.

The winner depends on the nutrient: hemp for magnesium, whole sesame for calcium and iron, with pumpkin and chia providing strong alternatives.

faq.question: Which seed has the most magnesium?
faq.answer: Among those compared, hulled hemp at about 700 mg/100 g, or 210 mg per 30 g.

faq.question: Which has the most calcium?
faq.answer: Whole dried sesame at about 975 mg/100 g, followed by chia at 631 mg/100 g.

faq.question: Which has the most iron?
faq.answer: Whole sesame at about 14.6 mg/100 g, roughly 4.4 mg in 30 g.

faq.question: Is plant iron absorbed the same as heme iron?
faq.answer: No. It is non-heme iron, and absorption is influenced by the meal; phytate reduces it while vitamin C can improve it.
